issues.legal_issue: A grant made as remuneration for village-office service is a service emolument, not family land merely burdened with service, and may be resumed and regranted when held by a person not entitled to its emoluments.
material_facts: The ancient grant provided land in lieu of wages or emoluments for the patel’s service and was independent of the village jagir.
Historical records and the parties’ statements in revenue proceedings described the land as remuneration for the patel’s work.
The claimant acquired the disputed land through a family partition but had never served as patel; the revenue authorities resumed it and regranted it to the working patel.
issues.conclusion: The lands were a service grant in the nature of emoluments for the office, not family property burdened with service; they could not be freely alienated, and the Government could resume and regrant them to the person entitled to the office’s emoluments.
issues.legal_principle: The distinction is between a grant of an office remunerated by land, which is prima facie resumable, and a grant of land burdened with service, which is not prima facie resumable absent terms or circumstances establishing that result: Lakhamgouda Basavaprabhu Sardesai v. Baswantrao. The historical documents and the parties’ understanding of the grant may establish its character when the original sanads are unavailable. The Inam Rules, 1859, and the Patel and Patwaris Law, 1900, treat service grants as emoluments attached to office and restrict their alienation; section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, authorises forfeiture and regrant in the specified circumstances.

predicates.civil_challenge_to_revenue_resumption: A person brought a civil challenge to revenue authorities’ resumption of land granted for village-office service.
predicates.service_emolument_grant: The grant gave land in place of wages or emoluments for performing a village office, rather than giving family land subject to a service burden.
predicates.nonofficiating_claimant_holds_land: A person who was not performing the office held land granted as its emoluments.

issues.definition: When a person challenges revenue resumption of land held as office emoluments but is not performing the office, the Government may resume and regrant that service land.

issues.legal_issue: A patel who is out of turn under a rotational arrangement does not thereby cease to be a patel or lose the emoluments attached to the office.
material_facts: Several patel families held the office in rotation for terms of ten years.
The patel’s inam land remained with each patel even when another patel was serving the current turn.
issues.conclusion: Rotation of the work did not mean that a patel ceased to be a patel when his turn ended; he continued to hold that status and enjoy the emoluments of office.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Patel and Patwaris Law, 1900, permits the Deputy Commissioner to direct rotational performance of the duties by multiple patels. Rotation of duties does not terminate a patel’s status or, by itself, extinguish his entitlement to the office’s emoluments.

predicates.challenge_to_rotational_office_emolument: A dispute concerns the allocation of emoluments attached to a village office held in rotation.
predicates.village_office_is_held_by_rotation: More than one village officer performs the office in successive turns.
predicates.each_rotation_holder_retains_office_stat: Each person taking a turn remains recognised as an office-holder after that turn ends.

issues.definition: Where a village office is held in rotation and each rotating officer retains office-holder status, the officer retains the emoluments between turns.

issues.legal_issue: A person is not entitled to a share in service emoluments merely because that person belongs to the office-holder’s family and another family member performs the service.
material_facts: The claimant was a member of the patel family but had never held the patel’s office.
The land was a service grant, and the claimant’s relative and later the respondent performed the patel’s duties.
The claimant relied on a family partition to claim the land as his share.
issues.conclusion: The claimant had no right, merely as a family member, to a share in the patel’s service emoluments, and the revenue authorities could resume the land and regrant it to the officiating patel.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Inam Rules, 1859, including Rules V, VI, VIII, XI, XIV and XXI, a family member has no right to share service emoluments irrespective of performance of the service; the rules address service grants as attached to office and restrict their division and alienation. Sections 9–11 and 20 of the Patel and Patwaris Law, 1900, provide for enjoyment of office emoluments by the person holding office, restrict attachment, sale and assignment, and bar civil claims to such emoluments. Section 192 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, excludes civil suits on matters entrusted to revenue authorities. Krishnarao v. Nilkantha concerned a jagir, while Mir Subhan Ali v. Imami Begum, Jaiwantrao v. Sahebrao and Raje Shrinivasrao v. Raje Vinayakrao concerned grants that were not service grants; those decisions did not establish a family member’s right to share patel-office emoluments.

predicates.civil_challenge_to_service_grant_allocat: A person brought a civil challenge concerning the allocation of land granted as emoluments for village-office service.
predicates.service_grant_governed_by_revenue_rules: The land is a service grant whose allocation and enjoyment are governed by rules for office emoluments and revenue administration.
predicates.claimant_is_nonserving_family_member: The claimant belongs to the office-holder’s family but does not perform the service attached to the grant.

issues.definition: A non-serving family member has no automatic share in a service grant when its allocation is governed by revenue rules.

issues.legal_issue: Land within a service grant does not lose its character as part of that grant merely because it was once included in a resumed portion of the larger jagir or because the claimant relies on decrees concerning other property.
material_facts: Two disputed plots fell within the portion of the jagir resumed earlier and were recorded as assessed land.
The later Government order excluded the patel’s lands from resumption and treated the plots as part of the same body of patelki inam lands as the other plots.
The decrees relied on by the claimant concerned property other than the two disputed plots.
issues.conclusion: The two plots stood on the same footing as the other patelki inam lands and remained subject to resumption as part of the service grant.
issues.legal_principle: The character and treatment of the service grant are determined from the grant and the relevant revenue proceedings. Where the revenue order treats the plots as part of one homogeneous service grant, their earlier inclusion in a resumed portion of a separate jagir does not by itself convert them into private family property.

rule.if: civil_challenge_to_resumption and plots_are_part_of_same_service_grant and earlier_jagir_resumption_did_not_end_service_grant and relied_on_decrees_cover_other_property

predicates.civil_challenge_to_resumption: A person brought a civil challenge to revenue authorities’ resumption of land.
predicates.plots_are_part_of_same_service_grant: The disputed plots were treated in the revenue proceedings as part of the same service grant as the other granted plots.
predicates.earlier_jagir_resumption_did_not_end_ser: An earlier resumption of the larger estate did not terminate the separate service grant covering the plots.
predicates.relied_on_decrees_cover_other_property: The decrees relied on by the claimant concerned property other than the disputed plots.

issues.definition: Plots remain subject to resumption as part of a service grant when they were treated as part of that grant, an earlier resumption of a larger estate did not end the grant, and the claimant’s decrees concern other property.

issues.legal_issue: Adverse possession does not defeat the Government’s resumption of land granted as emoluments for village-office service in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The lands were held as emoluments for the patel’s office.
A family member who had never performed the service obtained possession through a partition after the prior office-holder’s death.
The Government later resumed the lands and regranted them to the working patel.
issues.conclusion: The claim of title by adverse possession against the Government did not arise on the facts, and the claimant could not use it to defeat resumption and regrant.
issues.legal_principle: Once land is found to have been granted as emoluments for an office, the Court held that no question of title by adverse possession against the Government arose in the circumstances considered. The claimant’s success depended on establishing an independent right to a share in the service grant, which he failed to establish.

predicates.challenge_to_government_resumption: A person challenged the Government’s resumption of land granted for village-office service.
predicates.land_is_service_emolument_grant: The land was granted as emoluments for performing a village office.
predicates.claimant_possession_arose_through_family: The claimant obtained possession through a partition within the office-holder’s family rather than through performance of the service.

issues.definition: When a person challenges Government resumption of office-emolument land held through a family partition, adverse possession does not bar resumption in the circumstances stated.
